notes.meaning: Job begins his reply to Zophar, turning directly to the big debate between them. Instead of focusing only on his own pain, he sets out to show that wicked people often enjoy long, comfortable lives on earth.
Job asks his friends to give him their full attention without interrupting. If they truly want to comfort him, simply listening carefully will be the best kindness they can offer.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The ancient Greek translation turns this sentence into a negative statement, suggesting the friends offered no true comfort.

notes.meaning: Job begs his companions to bear with him patiently while he presents his case. Once he has finished laying out the facts, they are free to go back to mocking him if they wish.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Because the Hebrew verb for mocking is singular here, Job may be directing this remark specifically to Zophar rather than all three friends.

notes.meaning: Job explains that his real struggle is with God, not with human beings. He is pouring out his soul to his Maker, and because God seems silent, it is natural for him to feel deep distress and impatience.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Job may be pointing out that while human disputes can find sympathetic listeners, no one dares to show sympathy to someone who questions God.

notes.meaning: Job urges his companions to look closely at him and at the hard facts he is raising. Putting a hand over the mouth was a well-known sign of silent awe, showing they should stop talking and marvel at God's mysterious ways.
Job admits that thinking about the mystery of God's providence makes him shudder with fear. It terrifies him to realize how often the wicked thrive while innocent people suffer terrible losses.

Job raises a hard question that directly challenges his friends' claims: why do many wicked people live to old age and grow in wealth and influence? The friends claimed evil people are quickly cut off, but daily life proves otherwise.

Evil men often see their children and grandchildren grow up safe and established around them. This cuts Job deeply, since he has just lost all his own children while wicked parents watch their families flourish.
Job points out that the households of wicked people often enjoy peace and safety from harm. God's rod of discipline, which often falls heavily on the righteous, seems not to touch them at all.
Job notes that even their livestock multiply steadily without mishap or loss. Their cattle breed successfully, giving them steady wealth in an ancient farming culture.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Rabbinic tradition and modern translation notes understand the Hebrew phrasing to mean the breeding bull does not fail to do its work.

notes.meaning: The children of the ungodly are numerous and lively, running around outside like healthy young lambs. They play freely in good health, contradicting the friends' claim that the families of sinners are quickly destroyed.

These wealthy families celebrate with singing and musical instruments like tambourines, harps, and flutes. Their homes are filled with music and joy rather than the instant gloom the friends described.
Wicked people frequently live out their years in comfort and ease. When death finally comes, they slip away quickly without enduring months of agony like Job is suffering.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew expression can mean dying in a sudden moment or passing away in peaceful quietness, and both ideas fit the ease of their passing.

notes.meaning: In spite of enjoying God's rich gifts, these people tell God to leave them alone. Their daily actions and attitudes show that they have no interest in learning His ways or obeying His laws.

The wicked proudly ask who the Almighty is and what profit they would get from serving or praying to Him. Because they already have earthly comfort, they think religion is a waste of time and has nothing to offer them.

Job declares that the prosperity of evil people is not under their own control, for only God gives or withholds wealth. Even though they thrive, Job firmly rejects their lifestyle and wants nothing to do with their wicked ways.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin tradition reads the closing phrase as a prayer asking God to keep the plans and way of life of wicked people far away.

notes.meaning: Job questions how often the life and joy of the wicked are really snuffed out like a lamp. He challenges the friends' bold claim, showing that God does not always send instant destruction upon sinful people in this life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The word for sorrows can refer to sudden birth pangs or binding cords, picturing severe distress that rarely falls on the prosperous wicked.

notes.meaning: Job asks how often evil men are actually swept away like dry straw or chaff in a windstorm. While scripture warns that judgment will come, in everyday experience they often stand secure for many years.

Job mentions the argument that God saves up a sinner's punishment for his children. Job insists that justice should fall upon the guilty person himself so that he directly feels the consequences of his wrongdoing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Translators often add the words they say at the beginning to show Job is quoting a common argument from his companions.

notes.meaning: Job argues that the sinner himself ought to see his own ruin with his own eyes. A wrongdoer should personally drink the bitter cup of the Almighty's holy judgment rather than passing the blow to the next generation.
Job points out that a selfish sinner does not care what happens to his household after he dies. Once his own days are finished, the struggles of his descendants bring him no personal sorrow.

Job reminds everyone that human beings cannot give lessons to God about how to run the universe. God is the sovereign Ruler who judges even the highest beings, and His choices are far beyond human wisdom.
One person reaches the end of life strong, peaceful, and completely free from earthly troubles. This person dies quickly without enduring long pain or hardship.
His body was well fed and healthy right up to the moment of death, with strong bones full of marrow. His earthly life appeared blessed and comfortable from start to finish.

Another person spends his entire life in deep pain and poverty, never tasting the good things of this world. Human circumstances differ wildly, showing that outward ease does not prove whether someone is good or bad.
In the end, death brings both the prosperous and the suffering person to the very same place. They both lie down in the dust of the earth, and worms cover them alike without any distinction.

Job tells his friends that he sees right through their words to the hidden thoughts they harbor against him. He knows they are using their descriptions of wicked men to secretly accuse him of terrible crimes.

Job exposes what they have been whispering: they point to his ruined home and ask where the prince's estate has gone. By looking at his lost household, they falsely conclude that he must have been an evil oppressor.
Job urges them to ask everyday travelers who have walked the roads of different lands. Anyone with broad experience in the world could tell them that real life does not match their narrow theory.

Travelers confirm that wicked people are often spared when disasters strike in this present world. Their ultimate reckoning does not always arrive immediately, for God reserves their full judgment for a future day of wrath.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate this to mean that the evil person is spared and safely escorted away during days of calamity, focusing entirely on his present earthly escape.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An older Catholic commentary notes that while some read this as God guarding the powerful person from present harm, it also points forward to his final payment when God judges him.

notes.meaning: While a ruthless man is in power, almost nobody has the courage to call out his wrongdoing to his face. Because of his earthly wealth and influence, no human authority holds him accountable or repays him for his deeds.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Both questions in this verse are rhetorical, expecting the plain answer that no one dares to challenge such a powerful wrongdoer.

notes.meaning: When this powerful sinner dies, he receives a grand and honorable funeral. Instead of facing open shame, he is carried to an impressive tomb where guards or monuments preserve his memory.

The soil of the grave rests gently on him, and enormous crowds walk in his funeral procession. Millions have died before him and countless others will follow, meaning death treats him no worse than anyone else.

Job concludes that all the comfort his friends offered is totally hollow and useless. Because their claims about God's justice in this life are false, their advice can never bring true peace to a hurting heart.
